t: Split Array Into Maximum Number of Subarrays — Greedy on Bitwise AND
o:
We must partition the array into contiguous subarrays minimizing the sum of their AND scores, then maximize the number of parts among such partitions. The key observation is that the AND of the entire array, $A = \text{AND}(nums)$, is a lower bound for any single subarray's score (adding more elements to an AND can only clear bits), so the total score of any split is at least $A$; hence the minimum possible total is exactly $A$, achieved by taking the whole array as one part.

If $A > 0$, no subarray can have a smaller score than $A$... actually every subarray's AND has all of $A$'s bits set, so each part contributes at least $A$, meaning the only way to reach total $A$ is a single part — answer is 1 (Example 2: AND(5,7,1,3)=1).

If $A = 0$, we want as many parts as possible whose ANDs are all 0. Greedily scan left to right maintaining a running AND; the moment it becomes 0, cut there and reset. This maximizes the count because extending a zero-AND segment further never helps future cuts (Example 1 gives 3). Constraints ($n \le 10^5$) demand an $O(n)$ or near-linear solution.
k: The AND of the whole array is the minimum achievable total score: AND-ing more elements can only turn bits off.
If the total array AND is nonzero, the answer is forced to be 1; if it is 0, greedy cutting works.
When the total AND is 0, greedily end a segment as soon as its running AND becomes 0 — this yields the maximum number of zero-score segments.

a.i: Try all ways to split using dynamic programming: dp[i] = maximum number of parts for prefix ending at i with minimum total score. For each start j, compute the AND of nums[j..i] incrementally and relax dp[i] from dp[j-1]. Since scores are non-negative and the full-array AND is the global lower bound, this finds the true optimum, but it costs quadratic time in the worst case.
s: Let total = AND of all elements; minScore = total.
For each i, iterate j from i down to 1 keeping cur = AND(nums[j..i]); if dp[j-1] + 1 improves (score sum stays minimal via tracking best score too), update.
Track pairs (minSum, maxParts) lexicographically in dp.
a.t: O(n^2) worst case — nested loops over split points, though the early break when cur hits 0 often makes it much faster in practice.

a.i: The minimum possible total score equals the AND of the entire array. If that value is positive, splitting only increases the total (each part's AND is a superset of bits), so the answer is 1. If it is 0, greedily close a segment the instant its running AND reaches 0: any zero-AND segment can be cut at the earliest position where the AND becomes 0 without hurting later segments, since a suffix starting anywhere after a zero point can still form its own zero-AND segment. This one pass achieves the maximum number of parts with total score 0.
s: Compute total = AND of all elements.
Otherwise scan left to right with cur = ~0 (all ones).
cur &= nums[i]; when cur == 0, increment count and reset cur = ~0.
Return count (at least 1 since total is 0 guarantees at least one zero segment).
a.t: O(n) — two linear passes (one could merge them into one).

w: In an interview, go straight to the greedy: first prove the minimum total score equals the AND of the whole array (bits only get cleared by AND), then case-split on whether it is zero. Common pitfalls: forgetting the `total != 0 → return 1` case (e.g., [5,7,1,3]); returning 0 when the array AND is 0 but the greedy loop somehow counts nothing (guard with max(count, 1)); initializing the running AND to 0 instead of all-ones. Edge cases: single element (answer always 1), arrays containing zeros (each isolated 0 lets you cut immediately). Follow-ups might ask for the actual split (store cut indices during the greedy pass) or generalize to OR/other associative bit operations.
